findings.label: Use suitable amendments in suitable amounts
findings.text: The manual suggests organic amendments for nourishment, biological activity and water holding. It calls for low pollutants, no impurities, stable material and avoiding excessive doses; examples are 1–2 L/planting hole or 50 Mg/ha surface application, retaining those different application contexts.

findings.label: La Alcantarilla: fruit table and climatic context
findings.text: Table 5.20 gives rainfall 200–300 mm/year, minimum temperature of the coldest month >6°C, maximum of warmest month 28–32°C, mean annual temperature 17–19°C and evapotranspiration 900–1000 mm/year. Table 5.21 (summers 2022/2023) gives pod length 14.2 cm, pod weight 8.66 g, seed yield 16.39% and 100-seed weight 13.90 g; sample size is not supplied.

findings.label: La Alcantarilla: carob facilitates observed shrub establishment
findings.text: A seminatural carob population around houses and a stream has expanded irregularly along paths, irrigation channels and streams. Lentisco and acebuche have established under carob protection. Care is limited mainly to fruit collection. Alternate bearing is moderate, but crops are small or absent in most years. This is not a quantified planting trial.

findings.label: Buenavista: intensive production differs from restoration
findings.text: The case in Posadas has rainfall 600–800 mm/year and deeper soils, uses 1 m cubic holes with a 50% cured-cow-manure mixture, and phases planted in autumn 2022/2023. Selected cultivars include Sayalonga, Alexia, P14 and P17, with 10% of the two hermaphrodite cultivars for pollination. Production was not yet measured; the source anticipates 3–4 years. These practices are not recommendations for Almería restoration.

findings.label: El Rano: historical management and inconsistent rainfall
findings.text: El Rano (Ubrique, Cádiz) is a longstanding livestock finca with carob, wild olive and family crops. Accessible carobs are grafted and cleared; difficult areas remain seminatural. The narrative gives 800–1200 mm/year rainfall, while Table 5.17 gives 1200–1600. Do not silently choose one or classify it as an Almería case.

findings.label: Carob establishment spans years, not a single settlement event
findings.text: The general planting recommendations describe 3–5 years of establishment and advise 1–5 summer waterings during the first five years, without litres per event or an explicit annual allocation. Preserve that wording without inventing a per-year frequency or a universal dose.

findings.label: Las Labores: dryland crops and a restoration transition
findings.text: Las Labores (Albox) has 200–400 mm annual rainfall, Mediterranean IV1 climate, coldest-month minimum 2–4°C, warmest-month maximum 32–36°C, annual mean 17–19°C, evapotranspiration 900–1000 mm/year, shallow calcareous soils and rocky outcrops. The landscape is dominated by dryland woody crops. Carob was planted in 2010 at 6 × 6 m in areas of dead almond trees, as almond and olive productivity declined.

findings.label: Las Labores: planting, protection and grafting
findings.text: The case uses nursery plants about 1 m high, manual 40 × 40 × 40 cm holes, perforated 60 cm shelters, tutors, formative pruning and tractor cultivation every three years. It reports grafting local hermaphrodite cultivars in autumn 2024. These are case practices, distinct from the MR1 summary table.

findings.label: Las Labores: reported establishment and fruit observations
findings.text: The manual reports low losses, good condition, heights 3–5 m and normal diameters 10–25 cm, with alternate bearing. Table 5.16 (summer 2023) gives pod length 12.40 cm, pod weight 13.56 g, seed yield 16.39% and 100-seed weight 17.73 g. Its claim about production four years after grafting conflicts with the reported autumn-2024 grafting and harvest chronology; retain that unresolved.

findings.label: Las Labores: 400 litres is a seasonal total
findings.text: Deficit drip irrigation is reported from May to September, with a total of 400 L/plant over that period. The number of events and dose per event are not specified. The seasonal total must not be imported as 400 L/plant/event.

findings.label: An annual area allocation is not a per-event dose
findings.text: Table 5.12 describes establishment/production irrigation below 1500 m³/ha/year for the intensive MP4 model. It is an annual area-based allocation, not L/plant/event; the text does not provide an event count permitting conversion.

findings.label: MR1 restoration guidance retains its own assumptions
findings.text: MR1 recommends diverse, appropriate-provenance forest material, favourable deeper/moister microsites, autumn planting and low-density restoration layouts. Page 123 describes <350 trees/ha, page 124 gives <100 in generic protective restoration, and Table 5.14 describes enrichment <200. The table says no irrigation; this summary does not negate watering documented at Las Labores.

findings.label: MR1 reports variable survival in earlier restoration
findings.text: The narrative reports survival ranges of 18–30% at Guadiamar, 0–65% in Córdoba and 40–60% in Almería, citing earlier work. These heterogeneous reports are not a prediction for a new site. It recommends using experience from earlier afforestation to identify better microsites.

findings.text: The study sought orchard spray delivery from continuous ground supplies. Tests used water; pesticide tests were future work. It did not measure seedling establishment, root-zone irrigation or carob survival.

findings.label: Inspect reservoir condition after planting
findings.text: Monitor damage/degradation. Snow can damage lids and freezing can damage pulp walls; seasonal lid removal/replacement is a source suggestion for snow conditions.

findings.label: Degradation time depends on environment
findings.text: The report says experience with moderate rainfall was breakup in 1.5–2 years, but leaves semi-arid duration open. It suggests reservoir strengthening for wind, runoff, soil pressure and frost.

findings.label: LIFE describes a 20 L Cocoon
findings.text: The manual describes a buried biodegradable reservoir initially filled with 20 L, near-root delivery and shelter. These are source-described functions; trial outcomes and additional watering remain separate.

findings.label: The supplier annex describes about 25 L
findings.text: The Land Life Company annex describes wax-sealed recycled pulp/cardboard reservoir/lid and shelter; approximate 25 L fill and 1–3 months discharge depend on soil/climate. Rain/runoff can recharge it. This differs from LIFE 20 L wording.

findings.label: Monitor growth and vigor with their limitations
findings.text: The annex describes height, base stem diameter and vigor. Grazing can cause apparent negative height growth; shelters obstruct diameter measurement. First-year establishment is distinguished from later drought, grazing/fire effects.

findings.label: Mycorrhiza is a supplier-described option
findings.text: The annex suggests nursery/planting inoculation to improve access to moisture/nutrients; selected pages do not report a controlled inoculation result.

findings.label: Dry summers can require additional Cocoon water
findings.text: MENAQUA suggests refilling at an appropriate summer time and a removable access cover. This regional guidance does not promise one fill is sufficient.

findings.label: Observed roots differ from intended deep rooting
findings.text: The report notes roots tending horizontally below reservoirs and identifies downward rooting as an open issue. The supplier annex describes deep rooting as intended function. Preserve these as different statements.

findings.label: Healthy roots and planting material remain essential
findings.text: Supplier prefers trees under one year, containers at most 4 L and diameter under 15 cm, healthy shoots/roots and no serious circling/J-rooting. Shoots preferably under 40 cm; avoid voids around the root ball. These are supplier criteria, not independent efficacy results.

findings.label: Cocoon is described as single-use
findings.text: The source says no reuse is possible and describes degradation in soil. It reports €7.80 per unit for LIFE; this is a historical source-stated cost, not a current quote.

findings.label: Humidity and slope can limit placement
findings.text: The manual advises against very humid sites because deterioration can accelerate; steep placement can incline reservoirs and spill water.

findings.label: Cocoon requires suitable soil and species
findings.text: Supplier guidance: at least 30 cm topsoil; clear piercing rocks from top 25 cm; preferably deep medium-textured subsoil with replenished water; check salinity/chemistry for the species. A planting tool cannot make an unsuitable tree locally adapted.

findings.label: Cocoon summary has its own scope
findings.text: The method summary reports 1,993 planted trees,68% survival,49 L/tree and €109/surviving tree. It is preserved separately from the later dated results table.

findings.text: Table 1 describes a 2100×2100×450 mm hexacopter,12 kg airframe,24 kg maximum takeoff mass and six 24-inch propellers. These describe the experiment, not a purchase recommendation or operating authorization.

findings.label: La Alcantarilla connects MR 2 to Mojácar
findings.text: The selected page introduces La Alcantarilla in Mojácar, Almería, with mean annual rainfall 200–300 mm. Potential vegetation includes mastic/kermes-oak/wild-olive scrub and jujube thorn scrub. The current landscape includes esparto and lower-area greenhouse crops.

findings.label: Altitude depends on exposure and regional conditions
findings.text: The handbook gives an optimum 0–500 m and Andalusian occurrences up to 900–1000 m depending on latitude, slope and exposure. It reports stronger growth and fruiting on south-facing slopes.

findings.label: Carob companions are ecological associations
findings.text: The handbook names wild olive and dwarf palm alongside carob, with Quercus ilex, Phillyrea angustifolia, myrtle, terebinth, mastic and less often cork oak. These are source-described communities, not controlled evidence that planting every member together improves growth.

findings.label: Dew uptake does not offset daily losses
findings.text: Carob can increase atmospheric-water uptake as soil water decreases, but the volume described is insufficient to compensate daily transpiration. Dew capture should not become a substitute for establishment water.

findings.label: Mediterranean distribution with uncertain native limits
findings.text: The handbook lists broad Mediterranean distribution and cultivated occurrences elsewhere. It says the exact origin and natural Iberian limits are difficult to establish because of long cultivation; native Iberian status is questioned rather than settled.

findings.label: Grafted/natural fruit at El Rano, summer 2023
findings.text: Table 5.18 gives grafted versus natural fruit: pod length 15.6 vs 9.8 cm; pod weight 7.74 vs 6.56 g; seed yield 14.68 vs 23.95%;100-seed weight 18.09 vs 11.22 g. These are farm/harvest observations, not universal benefits or a controlled causal result.

findings.label: Almond and olive in an observed mixture
findings.text: Figure 5.40 describes carob mixed with almond and olive in easier-to-cultivate parts of El Rano. Harder-to-cultivate areas are dominated by adult carob. The caption does not establish a growth benefit from mixing.

findings.label: El Rano is a cultivation case, distinct from MR 2
findings.text: The selected page describes an irregular adult stand, including centenarian grafted carob and planned grafting of naturally dispersed young trees. Reported tree crop loads range 50–300 kg, with some alternate-bearing years. The municipality is not assigned from uninspected pages.
conditions: Do not transfer to young restoration plants

findings.label: Food and regeneration connect carob to fauna
findings.text: The account describes wildlife fruit use, palatable young leaves and easy resprouting as ecological relationships. It does not establish that browsing pressure is harmless during establishment.

findings.label: Resprouting and a tentative fire-related interpretation
findings.text: Vigorous stump/root resprouting after crown loss or cutting is described. The account suggests seed-coat responses to high temperature may delay germination until post-fire conditions improve; keep that interpretation tentative.

findings.label: Long fruit cycle and alternate bearing
findings.text: The handbook describes development after spring fertilization and maturation in August–September of the following year. Maturation overlaps flowering; resource competition is associated with alternate bearing.

findings.label: Hard seed coat delays germination
findings.text: An impermeable coat slows and spreads germination over time. Once broken, water uptake becomes faster. This describes a mechanism, without prescribing a particular seed-treatment procedure.

findings.label: Carob identity and form
findings.text: The handbook identifies Ceratonia siliqua in Fabaceae: evergreen, generally 5–6 m tall, reaching 10 m in its botanical account. Roots extend beyond the crown and penetrate rock fissures. These are source descriptions, not guaranteed dimensions for a particular planting.

findings.label: Occurrence and community altitude differ
findings.text: The normal community range reaches about 1000–1100 m, while occurrence up to 1500 m is reported at La Sagra, Huéscar. Do not collapse these different descriptions into one decisive altitude limit.

findings.label: A broad reported climate range
findings.text: Warm/temperate-warm climates are preferred, with cold-area occurrences on sunny exposures. Most favourable rainfall is 400–800 mm/year; examples extend to around 200 mm at Cabo de Gata and above 1000 mm at Grazalema. Occurrence is not optimal establishment.

findings.label: The factsheet explicitly connects kermes oak and carob
findings.text: Its vegetation section names carob with warm-climate companions mastic, dwarf palm, wild olive, Rhamnus alaternus,R.lycioides,Phillyrea latifolia and Osyris quadripartita. This is a sourced co-community link, not mere co-occurrence in a PDF.

findings.label: Growth pauses in drought or winter cooling
findings.text: The account describes rapid cambial-growth interruption under summer drought and winter cooling, resuming when limiting conditions disappear. It compares this with other oaks without quantifying a mixed-planting benefit.

findings.label: One species has multiple community memberships
findings.text: Kermes oak occurs in holm-oak, cork-oak and pine communities and can dominate coscojares. Its most-arid and acidic cork-woodland companion lists are separate source contexts, not one universal planting list.

findings.label: Kermes oak is a distinct checked identity
findings.text: The factsheet identifies Quercus coccifera L.in Fagaceae, usually a shrub up to 2 m and occasionally a small tree 6 m or higher. It retains coscoja, maraña, matarrubia, carrasca, chaparra and chaparro. Shared common names do not resolve another oak identity.

findings.text: The full fourth page is a Regiones de uso map with Andalucía as one yellow region. It is source regional context; no municipality-specific suitability or funding eligibility is inferred.

findings.label: Factsheet defines one regional provenance
findings.text: The description defines one provenance covering warm terrain below 1100 m on varied soils/substrates, based on population continuity. Its regional narrative follows Sierra Morena, Guadalquivir, Huelva/Cádiz coasts, eastern ranges and dry Almería areas. This does not make every location suitable.

findings.label: Kermes oak is widely represented in Andalusia
findings.text: The factsheet reports Mediterranean distribution, especially in the western basin, and every Andalusian province. It commonly inhabits dry stony ground, often calcareous but also siliceous. Paleobotanical dates in the text are not its publication date.

findings.label: Sourced classifications permit several memberships
findings.text: Pages 2–3 enumerate luso-extremaduran and bético/marianense/araceno-pacense mesomediterranean Quercus rotundifolia series; bético-algarvian thermomediterranean Q.rotundifolia; bético-gaditan wild-olive series; semi-arid mesomediterranean Q.coccifera; warm murciano-almerian lower semi-arid/dry kermes-oak series; and bermejense serpentinite Pinus pinaster series. These are source vegetation classifications, not single-parent plant identities.

findings.label: Varied stony substrates
findings.text: The source describes acidic/basic substrates and multiple soil types, often stony or shallow: lithosols, cambisols, vertisols and xerosols. This breadth is descriptive, not proof that any degraded site is suitable.

findings.label: Evergreen leaves and seasonal renewal
findings.text: The source describes leathery compound leaves, renewal in April–May and persistence around 15–18 months. Its reproductive account includes male, female and hermaphrodite flowers; most cultivars are described as dioecious.

findings.label: Table 5.19 specifies provenance region 38
findings.text: The summary names local origin from identification/use region Litoral suroriental andaluz(38), below 100 plants/ha and November–December planting. This is source guidance, not a legal nursery-procurement determination.

findings.label: Modest routine management after establishment
findings.text: The source generally describes no competition control, fertilization or formative pruning in this model. Table 5.19 also specifies first-year replacement of losses and occasional manual weeding. These statements stay attached to MR 2, not all cultivation.

findings.label: Water harvesting is central to MR 2
findings.text: For arid/semi-arid restoration, MR 2 collects runoff at planting points using suitably dimensioned dry-stone, gabion or earth micro-reservoirs. Water infiltrates near plants; retained soil and nutrients also help address water erosion.

findings.label: Restoration assemblage and biodiversity
findings.text: MR 2 names Aleppo pine, wild olive and fig with carob. The source says these plantings diversify landscape and can contribute to biodiversity and control of torrential processes at microcatchment scale. These are model-level benefits, not quantified benefits for every species pair.

findings.label: A dryland use case rather than universal suitability
findings.text: The model emphasizes Almería and occasionally Granada/Málaga, often below 300 mm annual rainfall. Establishment is complex and associated with water harvesting. Mild winters and a long warm season are part of its source setting.
conditions: Site design is outside the browser

findings.label: Autumn advice assumes no frost risk
findings.text: The narrative recommends autumn, warns against delay beyond January and highlights risk on very stony/shallow soils. Table 5.19 specifies November–December. The narrative expressly assumes no frost risk.
conditions: Avoid late planting, especially shallow/stony soils

findings.label: Fruit production depends on more than flower count
findings.text: Flowering is reported from July to late November, sometimes January. Both insects and wind pollinate carob. Climate, nutrients, soil and male-tree proportion also affect fruit production; limited pollination can contribute to fruit losses.
conditions: Species presence alone does not establish fruit yield

findings.label: Choose appropriate and diverse material
findings.text: For protection plantings, MR 2 recommends manual planting, appropriate seed provenance and genetically diverse forest reproductive material.

findings.label: Drought tolerance differs from establishment guidance
findings.text: The account describes adaptation to 250–300 mm annual rainfall while recommending establishment above 500–550 mm or with irrigation options. Adult survival in long dry periods does not guarantee unaided young-plant establishment. Autumn/winter rain matters.

findings.label: Seed persistence and mammal dispersal
findings.text: The cited account reports similar viability after 4 years while the seed coat remains intact. Mammals can disperse viable seeds, but many consumers expel seeds before digestion. Small mammals such as foxes are suggested as potentially effective dispersers, not a measured universal ranking.

findings.label: MR 2 planting preparation and support
findings.text: The handbook gives 60×60×60 cm holes, small-excavator or auger preparation (auger if soil is not very clayey), or manual work at low density. It recommends a plant-centred microcatchment and stone mulch; table 5.19 specifies perforated shelters and support watering.

findings.label: Carob soil preferences and drainage warning
findings.text: The source describes shallow calcareous/rocky occurrences, preferences for calcareous sandy or sandy-loam soil, and adaptation to some sandy, moderately acidic or stony soils. It warns against poor drainage/clay soils and qualifies salt tolerance as apparent.

findings.label: Soil biology remains incompletely described
findings.text: Carob interactions with soil organisms are described as little studied. The handbook explicitly says carob cannot fix nitrogen despite being a legume. These passages do not support a microorganism-treatment recommendation.

findings.label: Narrative and table give different stock formats
findings.text: Page 133 allows one-year forest stock above 200 cm³ but considers formats above 1000 cm³ more recommendable. Table 5.19 gives one-year 200–300 cm³,8–10 cm-high stock. The selected text does not explain this difference; retain both.

findings.label: Olive and fig can follow improved soil conditions
findings.text: The source says carob can improve soil physicochemical properties and infiltration, allowing simultaneous or progressive olive/fig introduction in this model. Retain the condition and rationale rather than a universal companion rule.

findings.label: Water harvesting may still need establishment care
findings.text: MR 2 mentions small establishment irrigations, protective tubes and stone mulch alongside water compensation. Its statement about generally low losses depends on favourable establishment conditions and care; it promises no survival at arbitrary sites.

findings.label: Carob distribution is temperature-sensitive
findings.text: Good vegetative/fruiting performance is associated with mean winter temperature around 10°C and summer means at least 20°C for four or more months. Frost sensitivity is emphasized. These are source ecology descriptors, not an automated threshold test.

findings.label: Young carob is particularly cold-sensitive
findings.text: The source says young plants may be damaged below 4°C and gives low-temperature intolerance in the ambiguous wording below 0°C(-4°C). Adults are described as tolerating summer temperatures above 40°C without apparent stress. The lower wording is not reduced to one decisive cutoff.

findings.label: Al Faisal almond survival remained low
findings.text: Both reported almond comparison treatments had 36.0% survival. The authors discuss dry-summer sensitivity and better-planned water supply; this is not universal device failure.

findings.label: Al Faisal carob was lost to flooding
findings.text: All fall carob plants were destroyed by canal floods and not replanted. Empty carob cells are missing results following disturbance, not a measured zero-survival Cocoon efficacy comparison.

findings.label: Al Faisal olive refill was comparable to irrigation
findings.text: At May 2020 monitoring, olive survival was 93.9% with Cocoon refill,92.0% without Cocoon/with irrigation and 72.9% Cocoon/no-refill. The source regards refill/irrigation performance as similar and the no-refill deficit as significant.

findings.label: Al Faisal olive water schedules differ

findings.label: Source-specific watercourse and jujube communities
findings.text: UAL describes warm Mediterranean watercourses with oleander and several Tamarix species. At Torre García, Ziziphus lotus dominates jujube scrub; Lycium intricatum is a companion and Thymus hyemalis occurs in openings. Its Tabernas discussion also names rosemary scrub. These are habitat descriptions, not mixed-planting trials.

findings.label: Ephedra cones and evidence limits
findings.text: Ephedra fragilis is dioecious; the female illustration shows fleshy cone structures, not ordinary fruit. The source describes green photosynthetic shoots and arid scrub membership, while noting that cited mycorrhizal evidence concerns other Ephedra species.

findings.label: Esparto leaves respond to water conditions
findings.text: The UAL account describes rolled leaves that reduce water loss and can unfold in wetter conditions, arbuscular mycorrhiza, and regrowth from underground parts after fire. It describes dry tussock grasslands from sea level to 1500 m in southeastern Iberia; this is not a planting-success prediction.

findings.label: Oleander toxicity is part of its plant profile
findings.text: The university botanical entry explicitly describes oleander as toxic if ingested. Its presence in watercourse vegetation is not a recommendation for unrestricted planting or use.

findings.label: Retama ecology and symbiosis context
findings.text: The UAL Retama account describes photosynthetic green shoots, short-lived leaves, Rhizobium symbiosis and arbuscular mycorrhiza. It places the plant in retama scrub and sometimes as a rambla pioneer, from sea level to 1500 m. These species-specific observations do not imply that every legume fixes nitrogen or establish a treatment recommendation.

findings.label: Winter thyme avoids summer drought through seasonal timing
findings.text: The cited subsp. hyemalis account describes reproduction before summer drought, subsequent summer rest and rolled hairy leaf margins. It explicitly lacks species-specific mycorrhizal evidence, although other Thymus species have been studied. No inoculation recommendation is established.

findings.label: Wild jujube provides shelter and supports soil formation
findings.text: The UAM factsheet describes the thorny deciduous shrub as shelter for animals and plants, with soil-formation and erosion-control functions. These are source descriptions, not quantified survival benefits for a proposed planting mixture.

findings.label: Allow establishment before severe weather
findings.text: The manual discusses moderate temperatures and adequate rainfall, with generic early-spring/monsoon examples. Local Mediterranean dates are not computed from these generic examples.

findings.label: Choose the method for the actual site
findings.text: Species, climate, soil, water availability/quality, topography, costs, resources, access and environmental effects matter. Biodiversity, monitoring and future resilience are also included, without selecting one universal best technique.

findings.label: Choose native combinations for habitat objectives
findings.text: Where restoration aims to recover habitat and biodiversity, the manual advises techniques and species combinations that encourage native species and diverse habitat for local flora and fauna. It does not prescribe a particular beneficial carob companion combination.

findings.label: Restoration methods should follow explicit objectives
findings.text: The manual names protecting soils/ecosystems, stabilizing pollution, carbon sequestration, timber production and leisure among possible reforestation objectives. It calls for explicit project objectives and suitable species/methods rather than assuming the same purpose everywhere.

findings.label: Plan supply and water-harvesting effects together
findings.text: Water availability affects methods, quantities and frequency. The manual also considers runoff captured by planting techniques, naming Cocoon and microbasins.

findings.label: Use weather and plant condition to consider support water
findings.text: Inspect forecasts and plants: prolonged dryness or widespread yellow/dry symptoms may justify additional watering.

findings.label: The LIFE control used holes and pipe watering
findings.text: The method uses 40×40×40 cm holes, no additional tillage and a stated minimum 1.50 m spacing. Shallow/stony areas need adaptation. These are project-method details, not a planting layout for a new site.

browse_groups.description:
Read watering evidence before selecting a planting example.

1. Nursery: watering before field planting, adapted to substrate, stock and growth or hardening stage.
2. Settlement: the first watering immediately after planting; it is different from all watering over the establishment years.
3. Summer maintenance: recurring watering during a difficult season, with a stated frequency and applicable period.
4. Support: extra water prompted by weather, soil moisture or plant stress. Support can overlap establishment and maintenance; it is not a final age stage.

Amounts and timing: L/plant/event means litres per plant for one watering application. Frequency says how often or what triggers it; period says when in the year; age context distinguishes nursery age from years since field planting. Unknown does not mean zero. A range is not a single recommended dose.

Read the context: soil, rainfall, species, nursery stock size, planting method and access to water affect the regime. Source recommendations, project choices and finca observations have different meanings. Generic LIFE NIEBLAS examples are not species-specific carob recommendations. Evidence does not automatically set a working community's values.

Compare like quantities: 30 L for 100 plants equals an average 0.3 L/plant/event. Container sizes in litres are not doses. A 20 L Cocoon reservoir fill is additional to settlement water. A seasonal total (Las Labores: 400 L/plant over May–September), annual allocation or tank capacity cannot become a per-event dose without sufficient information. No automatic age-based dose curve or stopping age is established.

Glossary: IND/IFWC means individual fog water collector. AFDS means Autonomous Fluid Discharge System: collected water fills a tank and its level triggers discharge through an irrigation network. The maintenance passage uses “SAD” without expanding it; its correspondence with AFDS is a curated interpretation of the matching operation, not a verified acronym expansion. MR means restoration model: MR1 recovers degraded areas; MR2 is oasificación, or restoration using runoff harvesting. MP means production model: MP1 enriches dehesas, MP2 improves older afforestation, MP3 establishes extensive production and MP4 uses intensive production.

Open a phase for quantities, frequency or trigger, season, age context, source limitations and exact-page evidence. Follow its connections to methods and fincas for the practical examples.
